investigacion.base:
**Snapshot as of October 6, 2026.** No ruling has happened yet, so the question can't resolve on current information. The hearing is still on for October 16.

**What the named sources say**
- **FITSNews (Sept. 30):** The defense filed a motion to compel evidence about the alleged crime-scene cover-up and disposal of the weapons, and asked McCaslin to take it up on October 16. FITSNews noted that whether the court hears or resolves every issue raised remains to be determined. The motion also asks McCaslin to preserve the newly sought records and allow the defense to supplement its pending dismissal and sanctions arguments.
- **ABC News 4 / WCIV:** I didn't find any specific coverage there. Sister stations (WRDW, WTOC/WIS, Oct. 2) carried the story.
- **Metaculus FAQ:** This is just the definition of "credible sources." It contains nothing case-specific.

**Key recent developments**
- **Sept. 18 motion:** It asks for DNA evidence from the body of murder victim Maggie Murdaugh, ballistic evidence related to one of the murder weapons involved, and high-tech, three-dimensional "FARO scan" data.
- **Sept. 28 motion:** It asks for the raw cellphone extraction files. The defense says it only got "reports" and needs the complete raw files in order for his own experts to conduct an analysis.
- **Sept. 30 motion:** It asks for the cover-up and weapons-disposal evidence.
- **Oct. 1 Harpootlian letter:** It says three defense "motions to compel" are still pending before the Court, and five written discovery requests to the State are still outstanding. It also says the State's only response was a Sept. 17 letter.
- **Oct. 2, McCaslin's notice:** She will hear all urgent evidentiary issues at the in-person hearing on October 16. The defense says the DNA, cell phone extraction, ballistic data, and FARO scan data will be addressed at the hearing. McCaslin ordered the State to submit their response by Thursday, Oct. 8 at noon. She said all other motions will be heard at the Nov. 13 hearing.
- That could mean the Sept. 30 cover-up motion gets pushed to November 13. Even so, the four categories still on the October 16 agenda are all motions to compel.

**Scheduled events**
- **Oct. 8, noon:** The State's response is due.
- **Oct. 16, 10 a.m.:** The hearing in Lexington.
- **Nov. 13:** A hearing on the remaining motions.
- **About April 5, 2027:** The retrial is tentatively set for that week in Sumter.

**Factors pointing toward YES**
- The judge set an expedited, narrowly focused hearing and gave the State a deadline to respond.
- She called the issues "urgent," and the trial date is getting close.
- Raw extraction files, FARO data and lab records are routine Rule 5/Brady material. Judges commonly grant at least part of requests like these, and a partial grant is enough for YES.

**Factors pointing toward NO**
- The State may hand over some material voluntarily, or agree to, before or at the hearing. That could make the motions moot, or the judge might only note an agreement rather than issue an order. The question's wording doesn't make clear how an agreed or consent order would count.
- The judge could take the motions under advisement, order the parties to confer, or set a separate DNA hearing. All of those resolve NO.
- The hearing could be postponed.
- A written ruling issued after October 16 may not clearly count, though the criteria allow written orders "in connection with" the hearing.

**Prediction markets:** I didn't find any.

**Current status:** The question is unresolved. Nothing is reported to have been ordered yet, so the status quo outcome would be NO until a ruling happens.

criterios:
This question resolves YES if, at the in-person evidentiary/motions hearing scheduled for 10 a.m. ET on October 16, 2026 before Circuit Court Judge Debra McCaslin at the Lexington County Judicial Center (part of Alex Murdaugh's murder-case pretrial proceedings), the judge rules on a defense motion to compel discovery and orders the State (the South Carolina Attorney General's Office) to produce, turn over, or permit testing of any additional discovery material requested in such a motion — such as DNA/forensic lab records or biological material, ballistics/firearms data, cell-phone extraction files, or FARO 3D crime-scene scan data. Granting even one requested category (in whole or in part) counts as YES. The question resolves NO if the judge denies all such motions, takes them under advisement without ordering any production, orders only process steps (e.g., that the parties confer, or that further briefing be filed) without ordering any additional production, or the hearing occurs without any ruling on a motion to compel.

Resolution will be based on reporting from [FITSNews](https://www.fitsnews.com/tag/alex-murdaugh/), [ABC News 4 / WCIV](https://abcnews4.com/news/local), or other [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) describing the outcome of the hearing.
letra_pequena: If the October 16, 2026 hearing is postponed, cancelled, or rescheduled such that no ruling on a defense motion to compel discovery occurs on or before October 16, 2026, the question resolves NO. A ruling counts regardless of whether it is delivered orally from the bench or in a written order, so long as it is reported as having been made at or in connection with the October 16, 2026 hearing. If the judge continues a motion, orders further briefing, or schedules a follow-up hearing without ordering any additional production/testing at the October 16 hearing, that counts as NO. Scheduling a further DNA-profiling hearing (as distinct from ordering the State to produce or allow testing of material) does not by itself count as YES. Rulings on motions other than discovery motions to compel (e.g., the motion to dismiss, admissibility of prior testimony, venue) do not count.
razonamientos:
- **Time left:** About 10 days, until the October 16 hearing.
- **Status quo:** NO. No additional production has been ordered.
- **Reference class:** For an expedited pretrial hearing on several motions to compel, I would use a rough, judgment-based base rate of **60%** for at least one partial production order. This is not a measured statistic.
- **NO scenario:** The State produces material voluntarily, or McCaslin directs further discussion or briefing without ordering production.
- **YES scenario:** McCaslin orders the State to turn over even one disputed file or record, or to permit requested testing.
- **Decisive technicality:** A partial grant counts, but a promise by the State to produce material—or a follow-up hearing without a production or testing order—does not.

The expedited hearing and multiple distinct requests make a partial order more likely than not. The State’s October 8 response could still narrow or moot the disputes.

Probability: 64%

(a) **Time left:** Ten days, until the scheduled October 16 hearing.

(b) **Status quo:** No additional discovery has been ordered. If the hearing produced no qualifying ruling, the outcome would be NO.

(c) **Reference class:** In criminal cases with several discovery disputes set for a dedicated hearing, I would expect an order granting at least one request in whole or part somewhat more often than not—roughly 60–70%. That is a judgmental base rate, not a measured statistic.

(d) **NO scenario:** The State produces material voluntarily, and Judge McCaslin asks for further briefing or schedules another hearing without ordering production.

(e) **YES scenario:** She orders the State to turn over raw phone or FARO files, lab records, or material for testing—even if she denies the other requests.

(f) **Deciding technicality:** An agreement between the parties or a further DNA-profiling hearing is not enough; the judge must order additional production or testing in connection with the October 16 hearing.

The focused hearing and multiple pending requests make a partial order more likely than not, though a procedural ruling remains a substantial possibility.

Probability: 68%

(a) **Time left:** The hearing is on October 16, 2026, ten days from now. Reporting from FITSNews and local TV should follow the same day or within a day or two. A written order "in connection with" the hearing could come shortly after.

(b) **Status quo:** No order has been made yet, so the default is NO. However, the judge has set an expedited hearing aimed at exactly these motions, so a ruling is the expected next step.

(c) **Reference class:** Defense motions to compel discovery in high-profile state murder cases, heard at a dedicated hearing with the State given a response deadline.
- Partial grants are common. Raw data such as FARO scan files, raw phone extractions and lab bench notes is routinely ordered produced under Rule 5 and Brady.
- Judges often rule from the bench, or put an agreed production on the record as an order.
- Full denials are uncommon when the request is for underlying raw data behind reports the State has already used.
- Taking motions "under advisement" with a written order later happens perhaps 20–30% of the time.
- Overall base rate for at least a partial grant, reported as an order at or around the hearing: roughly 55–65%.

(d) **NO scenario:**
- The State says everything has already been produced and offers to resend some files. The judge tells the parties to meet and confer and report back.
- The judge sets a separate hearing on full DNA profiling and takes the remaining items under advisement.
- Alternatively, the hearing is postponed for a scheduling or health reason.

(e) **YES scenario:**
- McCaslin hears argument on the DNA, ballistics, FARO and cell-extraction categories.
- She finds that the raw FARO data and raw phone extraction files are discoverable and orders the AG's office to produce them by a deadline. She may defer full DNA profiling.
- FITSNews and WCIV report that "the judge ordered prosecutors to turn over" the data.

(f) **Technicalities:**
- An agreement noted on the record, without an order, could arguably be read as NO. In practice, though, reporting usually frames these as "judge orders."
- Merely scheduling a DNA-profiling hearing does not count.
- A written order issued days later counts only if reported as connected to the October 16 hearing.
- The September 30 cover-up motion may be pushed to November 13, but the four categories on the October 16 agenda are enough.
- Postponement of the hearing means NO.

On balance, the judge called these issues urgent, she has already granted limited DNA testing in August, and the requests are for routine raw data. That favors at least a partial production order. The main risks are the matter being taken under advisement or mooted by agreement, which keeps the estimate moderate.

Probability: 62%
